app.notes:
### Fixed

- **An update feed that failed its security check read as "Are you online?".** When the update feed's signature didn't check out (the development feed's signature was stale for hours), every place that checks for updates said you might be offline: App settings' **Check for updates**, the setup screen, the firmware card (**can't check (offline)**) and the Development channel dialog, while Games → Proton install showed the raw English error. The app now tells the failures apart: no network still asks about the connection; a feed that fails its signature check says **The update feed didn't pass its security check, so nothing was installed. This is on our side, not your connection: try again later.**; a feed it can't read says so the same way; the Development channel dialog says when no development build is published yet, and the Proton install shows the same plain messages (the raw error goes to the log). All 7 languages.
- **Windows: a launcher the app started kept part of the app open after it closed.** A Steam the app reopened (after a Games change) or started for ▶ Play inherited the app's open handles, including a network socket it was listening on, and held them after the app quit. Launchers are now started through Windows itself (like a double-click), so they get none of the app's handles. Linux and macOS are unchanged.
- **Windows: the Games tooltip in the navigation rail mentioned Proton setup**, which exists on Linux only. On Windows it now reads "your games and per-game profiles". All 7 languages.
- **A new controller couldn't pair with all four pairing slots taken, and nothing said why.** With every slot full the board stops taking new controllers, so one doing Create + PS just blinked until it gave up. Pairing slots now says **All 4 slots are taken. To pair a new controller, forget one first.** (from the board's real slots; the Developer card's pretend controllers never count), and with the matching firmware the OLED's Slots screen says **All full: forget one**. The Guide's Pairing slots section says so too. All 7 languages.
- **Accent color → Desktop kept the theme's own accent (Light theme: green instead of KDE's pink).** The desktop's accent was only read for the **Match desktop** theme; with Light, Dark or Controller, choosing **Desktop** just dropped the controller's color. It now applies the desktop's accent in every theme (buttons, selection, highlights; the theme's surfaces stay as they are). The app also found KDE Plasma only through XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP, which is missing when the app is started by `systemd-run`, some autostart entries or Flatpak/AppImage launchers; it now also checks KDE's own session variables, and a kdeglobals file with Plasma or KWin running. The accent is read from KDE's kdeglobals first, then the desktop portal, then the system. If none can be read, the Accent color row says **Couldn't read your desktop's accent color — using the app's**. All 7 languages.
- **A firmware update that failed partway kept the board claimed, so trying again could fail too.** When writing the firmware stopped (a cable or USB hiccup), the app never let go of the board's update connection, so it stayed busy until you unplugged it, and the error was a raw USB message. The connection is now always released, also when the update fails, so installing again works right away; the message says in plain words that the update stopped, that the board is waiting in BOOTSEL mode, and that the app offers to install the firmware again (or to unplug it and plug it back in if nothing shows up). All 7 languages.
- **Failures that showed nothing now say what happened and what to do.** An error pass went through every error path in the app and the firmware, each now shown in plain words (all 7 languages) or logged on purpose. Fixed:
  - Apply and Undo on Games → Home: an error showed for a moment, then the rescan right after wiped it. A request the app's own check refuses now says so in plain words, not as a raw error.
  - A setting that can't be saved (App settings, the tray's toggles, the narrator, "Keep the app up to date?", Games consent) is put back, and the app says so. Games consent no longer changes the window before the setting is saved.
  - A game's page: creating or deleting a profile, profile edits, rating, tags and notes that fail to save; saving, updating or deleting a button layout.
  - A game's profile that can't go on before the game starts (its normal settings stay on), and normal settings that can't be put back after the game.
  - Download and install for an app update that fails: the banner used to disappear; it now says why until dismissed.
  - Controller info → Refresh with Sony unreachable now says so. Undo now says when restarting the audio service failed. The tray's slot switch, and links and launcher links that don't open, now say so.
  - The mic test and the Windows USB repair no longer get stuck on an unexpected error.
  - Your board's answers read in plain words ("couldn't finish that, for example saving to its memory") instead of "Command 0x04 failed". With firmware from this pass, a slot switch, forget or wipe, or Edge extra-button change whose save to the board's memory fails now says so, where it used to look saved.
- **With "Check for updates automatically" off, the app still went online for updates.** It looked up the firmware feed at every start, on the setup screen, after switching the update channel and when the Development channel dialog opened. Now, with the switch off, the app makes no update request at all (the update feed, the firmware on offer, the Development channel preview, Sony's controller firmware list) until you press **Check for updates** (or a check button that says it goes online, like the Development channel dialog's **Check the development feed**). The switch says so, and the firmware card shows **not checked (automatic checks are off)** instead of a version. The Games page's check for our newest DualSense Proton follows the Games permission, which names it. All 7 languages.
- **A firmware update could install an older build than the one it offered.** The offer came from a fresh look at the update feed, but Install downloaded from the feed of the last update check, up to 6 hours old, or the other channel's after switching. Install now downloads exactly the version you were shown and confirmed, checks the file against that version's checksum, and if the feed has changed since, installs nothing and says **A newer firmware appeared. Check again.** One update check also reads the feed once instead of two or three times. All 7 languages.
- **Games → Home: a game's big Continue playing tile showed a flat colored panel instead of its art** (Ghostrunner from GOG via Heroic: a plain red tile, though its cover showed in the grid and the list). The tile's own background color reset how the art is sized and placed, so the picture showed at full size from its top-left corner: for Ghostrunner's 2560-pixel-wide GOG background, a slice of flat red. The art now fills the tile like the game page's header. Both use one lookup: the game's hero art, else its wide capsule, else its cover shown whole on the right of a gradient in the art's color, else the gradient alone (also under any picture that won't load). A game page without hero art now shows its cover the same way instead of a blank header.
- **Linux: the controller's volume and microphone level fix didn't stick.** After **Turn the controller's volume and microphone level up to full**, they were low again after the next firmware update, replug or restart, and the change came back on Games → Home. Each time the controller's sound card appears, Linux sets it to the levels it last saved, and the fix only changed the current ones. Apply now also saves them as Linux's saved levels (one password prompt, the system's own; the fix says so first), so they stay full; while the app runs it also sets them back to full whenever the controller reconnects and says **Controller volume restored to full**. When they're full now but saved low, Games → Home offers **Keep the controller's volume and microphone level at full when it reconnects**; when they're low again anyway, it explains what lowered them. Undo puts back the old levels and the saved ones (the password prompt again). Linux only. All 7 languages.
- **Linux: the controller's microphone near silent and its volume low after every boot.** Linux's sound system never sets the controller's own hardware levels, so whatever was saved last stays: on one machine the microphone level was 0 (the mic looked broken) and the volume 80 of 100 (−20 dB). Games → Home now has a recommended change, **Turn the controller's volume and microphone level up to full on this computer**, when they are low; Apply sets them to full (your desktop's volume sliders keep working), Undo and the change history put the old levels back. It notes that **Microphone level** on your board, when above 0, sets the mic level instead. Linux only (Windows and macOS set these levels themselves). All 7 languages.
- **Windows and macOS: "Is the launcher installed?" never showed.** The check asked a Linux-only tool and took any error for "installed", so a game page offered launcher links that couldn't open and said nothing. It now asks the system which app opens the link (Linux keeps asking the desktop with your own home folder), so the hint shows when the launcher isn't installed.
- **A plugged-in controller that wasn't charging showed "Fully charged".** The DualSense says "full" whenever it stops charging on a cable, also below 100% (it pauses charging when warm), so at 80% the battery tile showed no mark and Controller info said **Fully charged**. One check now decides what every place shows (battery tile, Controller info, the status line, the tray tooltip): **Charging** with the bolt, **Fully charged** only at 100%, and **Plugged in, not charging** with a plug mark on the tile below 100% or when the controller's own USB cable gives power without charging. All 7 languages.
- **The microphone test played back while you were still talking.** It showed "Recording… speak now" from the click, before the mic was even open, counted its 3 seconds from the recorder's start call with nothing on screen to show the time running out, and played the clip in your ear the moment recording ended. Playback now happens only when you press Listen back, after the mic is closed and the recording is in hand, and the status line says when it's playing.
- **The microphone test's playback was very quiet.** The recording was played as captured, far below the speaker test's level. It's now brought to the same peak level as the speaker test tune (one shared setting), at most ×16 (+24 dB), and an almost silent recording at most ×4 (+12 dB) so noise isn't turned into a roar; it never clips.
- **Applying the graphics-mode change did nothing.** The app's check for actions didn't accept the new fix yet, so Apply silently stopped; it does now, with a test.

### Added

- **Echo cancellation for the controller's mic, on by default** (firmware protocol 1.17). The controller has its own echo cancellation, and nothing turned it on, so the PC's sound coming back into the mic (voice chat, the Mic Test's live loopback on a headset) was heard again, more the louder it played. A switch under **Microphone level** turns it on or off (on by default), applies at once and **Save to** your board keeps it; a game's profile can hold it too (an **Echo cancellation** chip). With older firmware there is no switch. The Mic Test still opens the mic raw (the browser's own echo cancellation stays off). The simulated board speaks protocol 1.17.
- **Microphone level for the controller's own mic** (firmware protocol 1.16). A slider under the Mic Test's meter in the Microphone panel sets the controller's mic level, 1 to 64 (its own scale, 64 = full), the same on Windows, macOS and Linux; at 0, the default, the controller follows the PC's mic level as before. It applies at once, so the change shows on the meter while the test runs, and **Save to** your board keeps it; a game's profile can hold it too (a **Microphone level** chip). With older firmware the panel says to update it. The test's meter is now named Sony's **Input volume** for screen readers, so it isn't confused with the slider. The simulated board speaks protocol 1.16.
- **Games: the right graphics mode per game.** Ghostrunner and Ghostrunner 2 start in DirectX 11 and grey out Ray Tracing ("The game needs to be started in DirectX12 mode"). A new recommended change, **Start … in DirectX 12 so Ray Tracing is available**, adds the game's own flag (`-dx12`) to its arguments: Steam's launch options (after `%command%`; PROTON_PREFER_SDL, the gamescope HDR line and your own arguments kept), Heroic's game arguments, Lutris's arguments. Your own mode flag (for example `-dx11`) is left alone and the game page says so; the page shows ✓ once the game starts in DirectX 12. Linux and Windows (Steam); on Linux the change mentions that DirectX 12 runs through vkd3d-proton and the first starts can take longer while shaders are built. Undo takes the flag out again.
- **About → Proton changes (Linux).** A third changelog tab next to App changes and Firmware changes for our DualSense Proton: what each build (GE-Proton11-7-DualSense, GE-Proton11-7.2-DualSense) changes on top of GE-Proton, in plain words, with its known limits. It shows on Linux, where Proton runs Windows games, like the Games page's Proton card.
- **Games (Linux): Turn on HDR for HDR games.** Games with HDR (Indiana Jones and the Great Circle, Cyberpunk 2077 and others on our list, or any game you mark **Supports HDR** in its page's Setup) said HDR isn't supported, because Proton runs them through XWayland. A new recommended change, **Turn on HDR for …**, runs the game inside **gamescope** (Valve's compositor) with HDR, full screen at your HDR screen's current resolution, and moves it to our DualSense Proton so adaptive triggers and haptic feedback work with HDR (Steam: `ENABLE_GAMESCOPE_WSI=1 gamescope --backend wayland --hdr-enabled -f -W … -H … --force-grab-cursor -- %command%` in the launch options, your own variables such as PROTON_PREFER_SDL kept in front and other wrappers inside; Heroic: its own Gamescope settings; Lutris 0.5.17+: its own Gamescope options with HDR). A gamescope line you wrote yourself counts as set. Each HDR game's page shows a ✓ / ✗ checklist of what HDR needs (Wayland session, HDR on for a screen, gamescope 3.15 or later (3.16.5 on GNOME), its HDR Vulkan layer, our DualSense Proton, the game set up), each ✗ with what to install or turn on, rechecked when the page opens, and **Set it up yourself** with the exact steps and a line to copy for your screen; Home → This computer has the same checklist under HDR. Screens are read on KDE Plasma 6 (`kscreen-doctor`) and GNOME 48+ (Mutter's display settings); other desktops aren't offered the change (the page says why). Linux only: Windows games do HDR themselves. Undo removes only this change.
- **Games (Linux): XInput-only games find the controller.** Games that only know Xbox controllers (Ghostrunner, Control) saw no controller with our DualSense Proton. A new recommended change, **Pass the controller to … as a standard gamepad (XInput)**, sets PROTON_PREFER_SDL=1 for that game only (Steam: in front of `%command%` in its launch options, your own options kept; Heroic: its environment variables; Lutris: its system environment). It's offered on Home for every installed XInput game on our list, and on any game's page when you tick **Controller not detected** in Setup. Steam games need it only with Steam Input off for the game; otherwise the page says Steam already gives the game an Xbox controller. Our DualSense Proton builds before **GE-Proton11-7.2-DualSense** ignore the option, so the change also moves the game to the newest installed build that honours it (GE-Proton11-7.2-DualSense or later, else stock GE-Proton) and says so; with neither installed, the page says what to install. If Steam, Heroic or Lutris is running, the review says it will be closed to save the change, then reopened, and the app does that itself (never while a game is running; Undo works the same way). Undo puts back the environment, the launch options and the Proton version.

### Changed

- **About → Firmware changes opens at once, and offline.** The firmware's changelog was downloaded from GitHub each time the tab opened ("Loading…", or an error without internet). It is now built into the app with each release, like App changes and Proton changes, so the tab makes no network request at all.
- **Less work in the background.** Three things kept running when nothing needed them: the first-run question about installing app updates checked every second for the app's whole life (now only until it shows, and not while the window is minimized or in the tray); the stick tests' circularity sampling ran 30 times a second while the window was hidden (now paused until it's back); and the tour's hold-to-continue ring redrew every frame on a controller step even with no button held (now only while ✕ or ○ is held).
- **Glass look: the game tiles' captions are glass over their art**, like a console's home screen. On Games → Home the Continue playing bars (Play and the play stats, or the title and Play) float over the tile's art as frosted glass tinted with the game's own color, with the same lit edge as the rail and the save bar; the art runs underneath. In the Library grid each cover's title sits on a glass-colored band tinted from that cover, drawn without a live blur so scrolling a big library costs no more than before. The text on them is checked to read at 4.5:1 over any art, light or dark; with the system's Reduce transparency on, the bands are solid. The Standard look keeps its plain bars. The covers' store mark no longer blurs what's behind it in the grid (its dark backing stays), so scrolling costs less in every look.
- **The controller view does less work while you watch it.** It redraws with every live input frame (about 30 a second), and the Buttons list, the saved button layouts, the stick curve graphs, a finished drift test's results and the drawing's trigger and touchpad lookups were redone on each of those frames although none of them depends on the input. They're now worked out once and redone only when what they show changes. Measured with the Buttons list open, the app's own script time per second drops by about a sixth.
- **Games → Home is calm when everything is set up, and says clearly when something isn't.** The four setup cards (Game setup, DualSense Proton build, This computer, Recommended changes) no longer sit between your recent games and the library. When nothing needs you, game setup is one line at the top, **✓ Everything is set up. Nothing to change.**, with your launchers, the DualSense Proton build and where HDR is on; it opens to the details (what checking does, the launchers and whether they're running, the Proton build, This computer with the HDR checklist, and **Change history** with Undo) next to **Rescan**. When something needs you (a recommended change, a missing or newer DualSense Proton, a ✗ under This computer, or an HDR ✗ while you have an HDR game) that part shows open at the top, marked **Needs attention**, with its action (**Review**, **Install**); everything else stays folded under **Details**. A change you untick stays in view until the next check. Windows shows the launchers only, as before.
- **Games → Home puts your games first.** **Continue playing** shows the games you played last with **▶ Play** right on them: the newest one big, with its artwork, when you last played and for how long, the next ones beside it (up to five). A tile opens the game's page. The **Library** heading holds the filters, each with its count (All, With profile, DualSense, Needs attention), Sort and Show, over the cover grid;
